title: Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC) Case
subject: TCC informal-procedure appeal testing technological uncertainty in construction paving work without expert witnesses.
keyPhrase: Paveit Construction v The King 2025 TCC
summary: In Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 129, the Tax Court of Canada dismissed an Alberta paving company's appeal and upheld denial of its 2017 SR&ED tax credit for mobile roller-compacted concrete work. The key takeaway for claimants in Canada: without proof of technological uncertainty, rigorously tested hypotheses and contemporaneous records, field trial and error will not qualify.

body.text: 1. Executive Summary & Case Background
Procedural History and Factual Context

On September 25, 2025, the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) delivered its judgment in Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 129 (Docket: 2019-3604(IT)I, heard under the Informal Procedure), dismissing the taxpayer's appeal regarding disallowed Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) tax incentives for its 2017 taxation year. Presiding over the matter, Justice John A. Sorensen evaluated whether the field-testing and concrete-placement process work carried out by an Alberta paving company satisfied the stringent statutory definition of "experimental development" under subsection 248(1) of the Canadian Income Tax Act (ITA).

The appellant, Paveit Construction Inc., is a paving company incorporated under the laws of Alberta and based in Slave Lake, which had 10 employees during the period in issue (Reasons, para. 2). In filing its corporate T2 return and prescribed Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) for the 2017 taxation year, the appellant claimed SR&ED expenditure deductions and associated Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) for work performed on an undertaking described as the Mobile Roller-Compacted Concrete (MRCC) project (Reasons, para. 3). Paveit Construction Inc. argued at the hearing that it collaborated with an unrelated company, Rock Solid Concrete Product Inc. (Rock Solid), which designed the compact mobile RCC mixer used for the Project and received its own SR&ED investment tax credit for developing it, to field test that prototype mixer; that this testing led to improvements in the process of placing roller-compacted concrete (RCC), a drier and stiffer mixture compacted with heavy vibrating steel-drum and rubber-tired rollers; and that Paveit's own contribution to the Project was process development (Reasons, paras. 3, 9 and 19).

The Minister of National Revenue, acting through the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), reassessed the appellant for the 2017 taxation year, denying its claimed SR&ED tax credit (Reasons, para. 1). Counsel for the Crown (His Majesty the King), Zakiyya Karbani (with Shalene Curtis-Micallef, Deputy Attorney General of Canada, as counsel of record), defended the reassessment on the grounds that Paveit Construction Inc.'s mobile RCC project did not satisfy the foundational eligibility criteria established under subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Specifically, the Minister assumed that the existing technological and knowledge base within the concrete placement industry was sufficient and was used by the appellant to carry out the Project, that the appellant relied on the Guide for Roller-Compacted Concrete Pavements (2010), and that the appellant did not formulate, plan and execute the testing of any hypothesis aimed at a shortcoming or limitation in the underlying science or technology of concrete placement (Reasons, paras. 8, 36, 45 and 47); at the hearing, Crown counsel argued that the taxpayer's work merely adjusted standard variables such as mixing time, material proportions and equipment configuration, which are routine operational improvements, rather than a systematic investigation carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. At the hearing, where Paveit's President and CEO, Robert Loroff, was the only witness and no expert evidence was led by either party, Mr. Loroff himself acknowledged that the field work involved a lot of trial and error; the Court nonetheless found him to be a credible, knowledgeable and forthright witness who candidly admitted unhelpful facts, so the claim failed for want of supporting evidence rather than for any lack of witness credibility (Reasons, paras. 5, 6 and 25).
Governing Canadian Statutory and Jurisprudential Framework

In Canada, the availability of R&D tax incentives is governed by a bifurcated statutory regime under the federal Income Tax Act. First, subsection 37(1) of the ITA permits a taxpayer carrying on business in Canada to deduct current expenditures—and capital expenditures, which were excluded for expenditures made after 2013 and restored by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3, Royal Assent March 26, 2026)—incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada, creating a non-expiring pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. Second, subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA enable claimants to earn Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) calculated as a percentage of their "qualified expenditure" pool, offering an enhanced ITC rate for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), for which it is refundable, and, since the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, for eligible Canadian public corporations, and a basic non-refundable rate for other corporations, supplemented by provincial R&D tax credit regimes such as the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (Form AT1 Schedule 29) and Quebec's R&D salary and partnership tax credits (Forms RD-1029.7-V, RD-1029.8.9.03-V, and RD-1029.8.16.1-V). Administrative compliance requires the timely filing of prescribed Form T661 alongside Guide T4088 protocols (and Form T2038(IND) for individuals, or Schedule T2SCH31 for corporations) within the statutory 18-month filing deadline following the end of the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred.

The gateway to both expenditure deductibility under section 37 and ITC generation under section 127 is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis" and encompasses three primary categories of eligible work: basic research, defined under paragraph (a) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research, defined under paragraph (b) as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and experimental development, defined under paragraph (c) as work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

For commercial industrial claimants like Paveit Construction Inc., virtually all claims are advanced under paragraph (c) of the definition as "experimental development". Once core eligibility under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) is established, paragraph (d) of subsection 248(1) allows directly attributable support work—restricted strictly to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—where such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the core basic research, applied research, or experimental development. Crucially, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes routine activities from qualifying as SR&ED through paragraphs (e) through (k), which disqualify market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

Because the statutory phrasing of subsection 248(1) requires judicial interpretation to distinguish eligible "experimental development" from excluded "routine engineering" or "commercial production," Canadian courts uniformly apply the five-question analytical framework established in the seminal Tax Court of Canada decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 CTC 2520, 98 DTC 1839 (TCC), subsequently endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in CW Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393. As applied in Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King and cognate contemporary rulings such as Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King, Willowglen Systems v. The King, and Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King, the Northwest Hydraulic test requires the taxpayer to prove, on a balance of probabilities, that its activities qualify as SR&ED, with the Court applying five sequential criteria (although the Tax Court has repeatedly held that the fifth, documentation criterion is not mandatory) (Reasons, paras. 31, 33 and 56). First, the Court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Second, the inquiry examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the Court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses. Fourth, the framework assesses whether the process resulted in a technological advancement. Fifth and finally, the Court considers whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested, and the results, was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed.

body.text: The Court's Final Holding and Broader Jurisprudential Context

In dismissing Paveit Construction Inc.'s appeal, the Tax Court of Canada held that the appellant's mobile roller-compacted concrete field process failed at every stage of the Northwest Hydraulic inquiry. The Court noted that the known parameters in making and laying concrete (hydration, proportioning, density, timing, haul distance and climate) are ones a person in the concrete business would be expected to know and balance, and that Mr. Loroff admitted relying on existing industry knowledge, including existing science on cement hydration and crystal formation (Reasons, para. 41). In the absence of expert evidence or other convincing evidence of a gap in existing scientific or technological knowledge, the Court was not persuaded that Paveit resolved a system uncertainty or went beyond routine engineering or standard procedures, so the requisite "technological uncertainty" was absent. Furthermore, the Court concluded that the hypotheses described by the taxpayer lacked rigor, that the evidence did not show a bona fide hypothesis being both formed and methodically tested, and that its work was substantially, and perhaps exclusively, trial and error rather than a systematic investigation governed by the scientific method (Reasons, paras. 46, 49 and 51).

The decision in Paveit Construction Inc. forms part of a decisive 2025–2026 jurisprudential trajectory in the Tax Court of Canada—alongside Vortex Energy Services Ltd. v. The King (2025 TCC 63, amended reasons issued May 2, 2025, dismissing claims for mobile direct-contact water heaters for the hydraulic fracturing industry), Tuna Temple Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 183, December 5, 2025, dismissing SR&ED claims for 13 projects across the 2005 to 2009 taxation years relating to the processing of super frozen tuna), and the partial dismissal in Willowglen Systems v. The King (2026 TCC 7, January 9, 2026, which cited Paveit on system uncertainty, rejecting the SCADACOM-5 supervisory control and data acquisition software project while allowing the SIL 4 Manual Train Control Logic Module project). Collectively, these rulings demonstrate that the Tax Court is enforcing an increasingly rigorous evidentiary demarcation between complex commercial engineering or field implementation on one hand, and statutorily eligible experimental development on the other.
2. Core Legal & Evidentiary Failures

A forensic examination of the ruling in Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King reveals five interrelated legal, technical, and evidentiary deficiencies that proved fatal to the appellant's 2017 SR&ED claim. Each failure reflects a recurring structural vulnerability among industrial, construction, and manufacturing claimants in Canada.
Failure to Establish Technological Uncertainty Versus Routine Engineering

Under the first prong of Northwest Hydraulic, a claimant must demonstrate the existence of a "technological uncertainty"—defined in Canadian tax law as an uncertainty regarding whether a given technical objective can be achieved at all, or how to achieve it, based on the state of generally available scientific or technological knowledge and standard practice in the industry at the commencement of the work. Critically, as established in Northwest Hydraulic, if a problem can be resolved by routine engineering or standard procedures known to a competent professional in the relevant field, no technological uncertainty exists.

In Paveit Construction Inc., the appellant sought to characterize the operational difficulties of producing and placing roller-compacted concrete via a mobile field process as a technological uncertainty. Roller-compacted concrete is an engineered mixture of aggregates, cementitious materials (Portland cement and supplementary cementitious materials such as fly ash or slag), and water, mixed to a zero-slump consistency and compacted via heavy vibratory rollers. While field testing Rock Solid's compact mobile RCC mixer with Paveit's paver on five jobs at client sites presented real operational difficulties (excess water that caused rolling problems and visible tracks, surface dryness and crumbling in heat and wind, seams between paver pulls, and component wear on the mixer), the Court was not persuaded, on the evidence led, that these challenges involved a technological uncertainty going beyond routine engineering or standard procedures (Reasons, paras. 15 to 18, 26 and 42).

The core legal failure lay in conflating project-level operational uncertainty or company-specific knowledge gaps with objective technological uncertainty. Whether Paveit Construction Inc.'s mobile mixer and paver process would yield higher-strength RCC depended on parameters that, in the Court's view, a person in the concrete business would be expected to know and balance (hydration, proportioning, density, timing, haul distance and climate), much as a photographer varies aperture, shutter timing and light sensitivity; the Court drew this context from the Guide for Roller-Compacted Concrete Pavements (2010), on which Mr. Loroff admitted relying, rather than from ACI or CSA guidelines, and also noted that Paveit's feedback leading to reinforcement of the Rock Solid mixer formed part of Rock Solid's own SR&ED claim and was excluded routine testing (Reasons, paras. 8, 39 and 41). The appellant failed to establish that its combination of known technologies, devices and processes was non-trivial or gave rise to a system uncertainty, a question the Court found difficult to assess without expert evidence (Paveit's agent could not act as both advocate and independent expert), and Mr. Loroff conceded that the work generated no new knowledge about concrete crystal growth or hydration (Reasons, paras. 7, 22 and 40). Where the solution pathways are already mapped in civil engineering literature and equipment manufacturer specifications, adapting those techniques to a company's mobile field operations represents routine engineering, which does not satisfy the technological uncertainty requirement that the Northwest Hydraulic framework reads into subsection 248(1); as the Court noted, citing Béton mobile du Québec Inc. v. The Queen (2019 TCC 278), the mere fact that a product does not exist does not by itself imply technological uncertainty (Reasons, para. 38).
Absence of Testable Hypotheses Targeting Root-Cause Mechanisms

The second Northwest Hydraulic criterion mandates that the taxpayer formulate specific hypotheses aimed at reducing or eliminating the identified technological uncertainty. In Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence, a valid hypothesis is not merely an engineering goal or a performance target, such as asserting a belief that modifying the mobile mixer feed rate will produce compliant RCC pavement. Rather, as the Court adopted from Maritime-Ontario Freight Lines Ltd. v. R (2003 TCC 674), a hypothesis is a tentative assumption or explanation to an unknown problem, ordinarily shown by a logical plan devised to observe and resolve that problem, within the Northwest Hydraulic five-stage process of observing the problem, formulating a clear objective, articulating the technological uncertainty, formulating a hypothesis designed to reduce it, and testing that hypothesis methodically and systematically (Reasons, paras. 43 and 44).

The Tax Court found that Paveit Construction Inc. did not meet the second criterion because of a lack of rigor in formulating a hypothesis: although Mr. Loroff described investigating whether reducing placement time would improve strength, and secondarily whether cement powder could be reduced and hydration managed, the evidence did not show a bona fide hypothesis that was both formed and methodically tested (Reasons, paras. 20, 46 and 49). When asked to identify the technological uncertainty, Mr. Loroff described a performance objective (achieving higher-strength RCC with a mobile mixer so that smaller projects in smaller communities could use the product), and the hypothesis advanced in argument by Paveit's agent (preserving crystal growth and managing minimum hydration) was drawn from high-strength results already achieved in the field (Reasons, paras. 19 and 47). In the absence of a rigorously formulated hypothesis, the adjustments made in the field (less water, different mix compositions and sealers, shorter paver pulls, faster compaction with a second roller and an imported European paver, and immediate sealing) could not be evaluated as hypothesis-testing experiments (Reasons, paras. 16 to 19). This mirrors the Tax Court's parallel critique in Willowglen Systems v. The King (2026 TCC 7), decided after Paveit, where the Court rejected the SCADACOM-5 project at the first criterion as product development using routine engineering, observing that SR&ED research objectives, while creative, must also be realistic, and contrasted it with the MTCLM project, in which each technological uncertainty was identified as it arose and addressed by hypotheses that were methodically and systematically tested.
Reliance on Ad Hoc Trial-and-Error Rather Than the Scientific Method

The third—and often most decisive—pillar of the Northwest Hydraulic framework requires that the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, characterized by a systematic investigation comprising observation, hypothesis formulation, controlled experimentation or rigorous mathematical and engineering analysis, data measurement, and logical conclusion leading to hypothesis modification.

Justice Sorensen concluded that Paveit Construction Inc.'s work was substantially, and perhaps exclusively, composed of trial and error, and observed that real-world testing with multiple uncontrolled variables looks more like trial and error than a scientific method (Reasons, paras. 48 and 51). In Canadian tax law, the distinction between systematic experimentation and trial-and-error is central to eligibility, although the Court acknowledged, following Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. R (2017 TCC 6), that trial and error may have a place within a broader and more structured methodology (Reasons, para. 51). Excluded trial-and-error is an intuitive, reactive process in which an operator or engineer encounters a performance issue in the field, alters one or more operational parameters simultaneously based on practical experience or intuition to observe whether the adjustment works, and terminates the inquiry once acceptable commercial performance is achieved, without isolating variables or analyzing the underlying physical mechanism. By contrast, the statutorily required scientific method is a structured, pre-planned protocol where independent variables are systematically isolated and manipulated against a baseline control, quantitative metrics are recorded across both successful and failed iterations, and the resulting empirical data is analyzed to validate or refute the governing causal hypothesis, thereby generating transferable technological knowledge.

In Paveit Construction Inc., adjustments to the mobile RCC field process were executed reactively during field deployments to get the equipment and mix performing to commercial specification. There was no evidence of controlled experimental design (such as Design of Experiments [DOE] matrices), no systematic isolation of variables (such as isolating heat and wind conditions from placement speed, paver pull length and water-to-cementitious-materials [w/cm] ratios), and no analytical root-cause deduction following unsuccessful field runs. When a taxpayer modifies field parameters on the fly to complete a paving process without a structured experimental protocol, the Tax Court treats the activity as trial and error outside the total discipline of the scientific method, as in Paveit, where Mr. Loroff described repairing failed sections by saw cutting and, in one case, covering a damaged surface with asphalt for the client (Reasons, paras. 25 and 51).
Failure to Demonstrate Technological Advancement

Under the fourth Northwest Hydraulic criterion, the process must seek to achieve a "technological advancement"—that is, an advancement in the general understanding of technology or science known to someone skilled in the art, rather than merely advancing the taxpayer's own internal capability or building a commercially viable asset. While a project does not need to succeed commercially to generate a technological advancement (as proving that a hypothesized technological pathway is scientifically unviable also advances the knowledge base), the work must generate new technological knowledge that was not previously deducible from established industry practice.

The Court held that, because Paveit Construction Inc. had not established a technological uncertainty that was a gap in existing scientific or technological knowledge, a technological advancement could not be found, and because no hypothesis meeting the second criterion was formulated, no advancement could arise from the rejection of a hypothesis either (Reasons, paras. 54 and 55). Mr. Loroff conceded that the work applied known principles to optimizing mixing and placement and generated no new knowledge about crystal growth or hydration; although he maintained that achieving additional strength with lower water and rapid compaction was an industry first, the weight of that evidence was reduced by his admission that he had not read the whole Guide (Reasons, paras. 22 and 40). The Project results did not appear in technical journals or lead to patents, industry standards or published documentation, and nothing documented showed a benefit beyond Paveit Construction Inc.'s own operations; such corporate learning (know-how) does not equate to a technological advancement under subsection 248(1) of the ITA (Reasons, paras. 23 and 24).
Insufficient Contemporaneous Documentation, Credibility Deficits, and Commercial Production Overlap

The fifth Northwest Hydraulic factor examines whether a detailed record of the hypotheses tested and the results achieved was maintained contemporaneously as the work progressed. While the Tax Court recognizes that subsection 248(1) does not expressly require documentation, that the fifth criterion is not mandatory, and that the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada left room for oral evidence where the absence of records is explained (for example, accidentally destroyed notes) or for systematic research to be inferred where an advancement was achieved, contemporaneous documentation remains the only sure-fire evidentiary vehicle (Reasons, para. 56) to discharge the taxpayer's legal burden of proof.

In Paveit Construction Inc., the absence of rigorous, contemporaneous experimental records—such as dated laboratory or field test logs, hypothesis tracking sheets, systematic mix-design variance matrices, and quantitative failure analyses—weighed against the appellant: apart from tables of 28-day strength results from Paveit and Rock Solid and some basic journal entries by Mr. Loroff, no notes, test sheets or data logs showed how results compared to hypotheses, and these records had never existed rather than having been lost (Reasons, paras. 20, 24, 27 and 57). Furthermore, the Court found no credibility problem: it described Mr. Loroff as credible, knowledgeable and forthright, but his candid admissions on cross-examination (that Paveit relied on existing industry knowledge, that he had not read all of the Guide, and that results were not tracked in a journal) reduced the weight of the evidence supporting the claim, and the commentary of Paveit's agent, who had prepared the claim, was treated as argument rather than evidence (Reasons, paras. 6, 7, 13, 21 and 28). When a claimant attempts to retroactively re-characterize routine field construction logs or standard commercial paving jobs as "experimental development" years after the taxation year has closed, oral testimony must carry the burden on its own; in Paveit, where no such records had ever existed and no explanation such as accidentally destroyed notes was offered, the Court held that the documentation fell short of what would reasonably be expected (Reasons, paras. 56 and 57).

Additionally, conducting putative R&D within a "field process" during active construction operations can attract scrutiny under the commercial production exclusion under paragraph 248(1)(i) and the contract payment rules under subsections 127(9) and 127(18) of the ITA. In Paveit, the five test jobs were conducted at client sites and appear to have been commercial jobs, but the respondent did not argue the paragraph 248(1)(i) commercial production exclusion and the Court, deciding the appeal solely under paragraph (c), did not address contract payments (Reasons, paras. 15 and 30, footnote 7); as a general matter, however, when field trials are performed on commercial paving sites or result in usable concrete infrastructure for customers without clear physical, financial, and contractual segregation between experimental trial slabs and commercial deliverables, the expenditures may be either disqualified outright as routine commercial production or reduced dollar-for-dollar as "contract payments" received for work performed for arm's-length clients.
3. Comparative Summary Table

The following table maps each statutory and jurisprudential requirement under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act and the Northwest Hydraulic framework against the specific deficiencies identified in Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King and the evidentiary standard of proof enforced by the Tax Court of Canada.

headers: Taxpayer's Specific Failure in Paveit Construction Inc. (2025 TCC 129)
Tax Court of Canada's Standard of Proof & Evidentiary Benchmark

cells: 1. Technological Risk or Uncertainty
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 1

Admitted reliance on existing industry knowledge (including cement hydration and crystal formation science and the 2010 Guide) for mobile roller-compacted concrete (RCC); led no expert evidence, so the Court was not persuaded that combining known technologies created a system uncertainty beyond routine engineering; feedback on the Rock Solid mixer was part of Rock Solid's own SR&ED claim and excluded routine testing (Reasons, paras. 39 to 42).

The claimant must prove via objective baseline evidence (literature reviews, industry standards, engineering gap analyses) that a system-level constraint or scientific limitation existed that a competent professional skilled in the art could not resolve using standard procedures or routine engineering, and that the gap lies in existing knowledge rather than merely being unknown to the claimant; expert evidence is generally helpful (Reasons, paras. 35 and 42).
2. Formulation of Specific Hypotheses
ITA s. 248(1); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 2

Hypotheses described (shorter placement time improves strength; less cement powder; hydration management) lacked rigor and were not shown to be formed and then methodically tested; the stated uncertainty was a performance goal of higher-strength RCC with a mobile mixer for smaller communities (Reasons, paras. 19, 20, 46 and 49).

Following Maritime-Ontario Freight Lines and Northwest Hydraulic, the claimant must show a hypothesis, meaning a tentative assumption or explanation to an unknown problem supported by a logical plan to observe and resolve it, that follows from an observed problem, a clear objective and an articulated technological uncertainty (Reasons, paras. 43 and 44); a well-drafted hypothesis can take the form of a pre-experimental causal proposition ("If variable X is altered via mechanism Y, then physical property Z will respond by a measurable change Δ because of principle P") specifically designed to reduce or eliminate the identified technological uncertainty.
3. Systematic Investigation (Scientific Method)
ITA s. 248(1) ("systematic investigation or search... by means of experiment or analysis"); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 3
Executed reactive, ad hoc trial-and-error adjustments in the field rather than following the scientific method; failed to isolate variables or conduct controlled, repeatable experimentation.

The claimant must demonstrate adherence to the total discipline of the scientific method: structured experimental protocols, isolation of independent variables against controls, quantitative measurement of outcomes, and analytical feedback loops that modify the hypothesis based on empirical data.
4. Technological Advancement
ITA s. 248(1)(c) ("achieving technological advancement"); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 4

Generated internal corporate "know-how" and operational proficiency using existing RCC knowledge; because no technological uncertainty or properly formulated hypothesis was established, neither an advancement nor a rejected hypothesis could be found, and no results were published, patented or shown to benefit anyone beyond Paveit (Reasons, paras. 23, 24, 54 and 55).

The claimant must prove that the investigation yielded new technological knowledge (whether via successful validation or conclusive refutation of a hypothesis) that advances the technological baseline beyond standard industry practice.
5. Contemporaneous Documentation & Witness Credibility
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. Canada (FCA); Northwest Hydraulic Criterion 5

Lacked contemporaneous experimental logs recording hypotheses and systematic test results as the work progressed; had only tables of strength results and some basic journal entries, the detailed records never having existed; the witness was found credible, but his candid admissions limited the weight of the oral evidence (Reasons, paras. 6, 27 and 57).

Documentation is not a mandatory criterion, but documentary evidence revealing the logical progression between tests is the only sure-fire way to prove systematic research, and oral evidence may suffice only if the absence of records is explained (Reasons, para. 56); in practice the claimant should produce dated, contemporaneous documentary artifacts generated during the experimental process (e.g., lab notebooks, DOE matrices, test telemetry, failure analysis reports) that corroborate oral testimony and link claimed labour/material costs directly to eligible SR&ED.
6. Demarcation from Commercial Production & Contract Payments
ITA s. 248(1)(i) (commercial use exclusion); s. 127(9) (contract payment definition) & s. 127(18) (reduction of qualified expenditures)

Attempted to claim a "field process" integrated with five test jobs at client sites that appear to have been commercial jobs, without isolating experimental test beds; however, the respondent did not argue the paragraph (i) exclusion, and the Court relied on neither it nor the contract payment rules (Reasons, para. 15 and footnote 7).

Not decided in Paveit; as prudent practice, the claimant should maintain strict physical, temporal, accounting, and contractual separation between commercial production/client deliverables and experimental development, ensuring that the claimant bears the financial and technical risk and retains IP ownership.

body.text: 4. Two Applied Remedial Case Studies

To assist Canadian tax practitioners, R&D counsel, and technical directors in translating the judicial lessons of Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King into audit-proof compliance strategies, this section constructs two detailed industry case studies. Both case studies involve industrial and civil engineering projects that face the exact legal and evidentiary pitfalls identified by Justice Sorensen—namely, field-based process development, reliance on established industry knowledge, ad hoc trial-and-error, and lack of contemporaneous hypothesis tracking, together with commercial production entanglement (a risk present on the Paveit facts but not argued by the Crown or decided by the Court)—and demonstrate step-by-step how to restructure the projects to satisfy subsection 248(1) of the ITA and the Northwest Hydraulic criteria.
Case Study 1: Sub-Zero Mobile Geopolymer Concrete & High-SCM Roller-Compacted Concrete Field Process (Civil & Materials Engineering)
Scenario & Vulnerability Profile

In this first remedial scenario, Boreal Civil Materials Inc. ("Boreal"), a Canadian-Controlled Private Corporation (CCPC) headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, specializes in heavy industrial paving and remote infrastructure construction. Boreal seeks to develop a continuous mobile pugmill batching and placement system for an ultra-low-carbon Roller-Compacted Concrete (RCC) incorporating 75% high-calcium Class C fly ash and calcined clay supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) activated by an alkaline silicate-carbonate solution, designed to be mixed and compacted in sub-zero ambient conditions (−25 °C to −5 °C) for remote resource access roads.

In its initial unguided operational posture, Boreal replicates the exact vulnerabilities exposed in Paveit Construction Inc.. Boreal's field crew mobilizes a commercial mobile pugmill to an active client logging-road site in November. When the high-SCM RCC mix experiences flash-setting in the pugmill auger on the first day and fails to reach required 7-day compressive strength (20 MPa) due to freezing on the second day, the site superintendent reactively adjusts the hot-water feed temperature, alters the admixture dosage on the fly, and increases vibratory roller passes until the pavement hardens acceptably. Boreal then bills the client for the completed road section and files a Form T661 claiming 100% of the field crew's wages and concrete materials. Under Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King, this claim would likely be disallowed by the CRA and the Tax Court as routine trial-and-error field adaptation, and it would also be exposed to commercial production and contract payment arguments that the Crown did not raise in Paveit.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Project Governance & Baseline Technological Due Diligence (Establishing Criterion 1)

Before any field equipment is mobilized, Boreal must establish a formal SR&ED Project Governance Charter overseen by a qualified Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) or materials scientist. To prove that the project does not rely on "established industry knowledge"—the primary fatal flaw in Paveit Construction Inc.—the technical lead must compile a Contemporaneous Baseline Technology and Literature Review Dossier prior to commencing experiments. This dossier must explicitly document standard ACI 327R (Guide to Roller-Compacted Concrete Pavements), ACI 306R (Cold Weather Concreting), and CSA A23.1 standards, alongside peer-reviewed literature on alkali-activated high-SCM binders.

Within this baseline dossier, the engineer must articulate precisely why standard practice fails by isolating the system-level technological uncertainty. Specifically, while conventional chemical accelerators such as calcium nitrite prevent freezing in standard Portland cement RCC, introducing alkaline activators into a 75% Class C fly ash and calcined clay matrix inside a high-shear mobile pugmill at −15 °C induces a competing thermodynamic conflict. Raising activator molarity to sustain exothermic reaction kinetics at −15 °C triggers premature calcium-aluminosilicate-hydrate (C-A-S-H) gelation within 4 minutes, destroying the 45-minute zero-slump workability window required for haulage and vibratory roller compaction; conversely, retarding the reaction with polycarboxylate ether (PCE) superplasticizers or citric acid causes pore-water ice lens formation prior to matrix percolation, reducing 28-day flexural strength by over 40%. Documenting this thermodynamic antagonism between sub-zero freeze protection, mobile pugmill shear kinetics, and zero-slump compaction workability establishes an objective technological uncertainty that cannot be resolved by routine concrete engineering.
Step 2: Structuring Formal Hypotheses & Experimental Protocols (Establishing Criteria 2 & 3)

To eliminate any judicial finding of "trial and error," Boreal must prohibit ad hoc field adjustments and institute a gated, multi-phase experimental protocol governed by the scientific method. Every experimental phase must be preceded by a written Hypothesis Formulation Sheet signed and dated by the lead P.Eng. For example, in Hypothesis H-01, Boreal formally states that encapsulating a sodium metasilicate activator within a shear-degradable micro-crystallized wax-stearate coating (particle size 50–150 µm) at a 2.5% binder mass ratio, combined with a binary potassium carbonate anti-freeze depressant, will delay exotic alkali dissolution during the first 180 seconds of high-shear pugmill mixing, thereby extending the zero-slump Vebe compaction window to 45 minutes at −15 °C ambient temperature while maintaining an internal hydration exotherm of at least +5 °C for 72 hours to achieve 20 MPa 7-day compressive strength without thermal blankets.

Rather than executing random adjustments on an active commercial job site, Boreal implements a rigorous Design of Experiments (DOE) isolation protocol by constructing a dedicated, non-commercial 30 m × 40 m experimental test pad at its Slave Lake or Edmonton yard (or a segregated, non-billable test strip) divided into 12 isolated 10 m × 10 m test cells. Across these cells, Boreal executes a 2³ full-factorial DOE matrix systematically varying three independent variables across 8 test cells plus 4 control cells: micro-capsule wall-to-core mass ratio (1:1 versus 2:1), pugmill shaft rotational shear velocity (60 rpm versus 120 rpm), and potassium carbonate pore-fluid molarity (1.0 M versus 2.0 M), while holding aggregate gradation, water-to-binder ratio (0.32), and vibratory roller frequency (40 Hz, 4 static plus 2 vibratory passes) strictly constant.
Step 3: Contemporaneous Documentation & Instrumentation Architecture (Establishing Criteria 4 & 5)

To avoid the documentation and evidentiary-weight failures noted in Paveit Construction Inc. and Tuna Temple Inc., Boreal implements automated and standardized contemporaneous record-keeping throughout every trial. Each test cell is instrumented to capture quantitative empirical data, including embedded wireless maturity thermocouples logging internal concrete temperature every 5 minutes for 28 days, nuclear densometer compaction readings after each roller pass, Modified Vebe time consistency measurements (ASTM C1170) at 0, 15, 30 and 45 minutes, and core-drilled cylinders tested at 1, 7, and 28 days for compressive strength (CSA A23.2-9C) alongside scanning electron microscopy (SEM) micro-crack analysis.

Crucially, Boreal documents its analytical feedback loops. For every failed test cell—such as Cell #3, where premature capsule rupture at 120 rpm caused auger binding—the supervising P.Eng. drafts a dated Experimental Analysis and Hypothesis Modification Memo calculating the specific shear stress (in kPa) inside the pugmill and reformulating Hypothesis H-02 for the subsequent experimental iteration. Simultaneously, Boreal enforces strict SR&ED time and cost segregation: field operators and engineers log their hours daily into specific SR&ED task codes linked directly to DOE test runs (such as SRED-2026-RCC-EXP04), segregated completely from commercial paving project codes, while material invoices for experimental test pads are tagged as "materials transformed" under Form T661 Line 325 and failed trial slabs are demolished or retained solely for freeze-thaw durability monitoring.
Step 4: Contractual & Financial Restructuring (Overcoming Commercial & Contract Payment Exclusions)

If Boreal conducts field validation trials on a third-party industrial site, it must restructure its commercial contracts to prevent the CRA from disqualifying the work as commercial production under paragraph 248(1)(i) or reducing the qualified expenditure pool under subsection 127(18) of the ITA by contract payments as defined in subsection 127(9). Boreal achieves this through bifurcated contracting, executing a separate Experimental Field Trial Access Agreement distinct from its standard Master Construction Agreement. Under the Access Agreement, the site owner grants Boreal a licence to pour a non-structural, non-critical 50 m experimental test strip at Boreal's sole financial cost and risk. The contract explicitly stipulates that Boreal receives $0.00 in remuneration for the experimental test strip, that Boreal is contractually obligated at its own expense to excavate and replace the experimental RCC strip with standard commercial concrete if it fails to meet structural specifications, and that all intellectual property, mix-design formulations, and experimental data generated during the trial vest exclusively in Boreal.

body.text: Case Study 2: Automated Rheological Feedback & Inline Microwave Moisture-Compensation System for Mobile Volumetric Batching (Industrial Mechatronics & Control Systems)
Scenario & Vulnerability Profile

In this second remedial scenario, Prairie Volumetric Systems Ltd. ("Prairie"), a mid-sized industrial equipment fabricator and specialty concrete technology firm operating in Saskatchewan and Alberta, undertakes an industrial mechatronics and control-systems initiative. Prairie seeks to develop a real-time, closed-loop mechatronic control system for mobile continuous volumetric concrete mixers that integrates high-frequency microwave dielectric moisture sensors in the sand and aggregate feed hoppers with inline auger torque transducers to automatically adjust water and chemical admixture metering pumps within a 200 ms latency loop, thereby maintaining constant concrete rheology despite rapid fluctuations in stockpile aggregate moisture and fines content.

Without proper tax and legal structuring, Prairie falls directly into the evidentiary traps highlighted in Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King and the SCADA monitoring rejection in Willowglen Systems v. The King. In its unguided approach, Prairie purchases commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) microwave moisture probes, programmable logic controllers (PLCs), and variable frequency drives (VFDs), bolts them onto a mobile mixer, and spends eight months tweaking PLC proportional-integral-derivative (PID) gain parameters in the field while pouring concrete for commercial customers. Whenever sensor noise causes erratic water dosing, the technicians manually override the PLC, yet Prairie subsequently claims the entire eight-month software and mechanical integration effort as SR&ED on Form T661. Following Paveit and Willowglen, the CRA and the Tax Court would disallow the claim in full because integrating COTS sensors with a PLC via standard PID tuning relies on established control-systems engineering and trial-and-error debugging rather than resolving a genuine technological uncertainty via the scientific method.
Step-by-Step Remedial Restructuring
Step 1: Isolating Eligible Core Experimental Development from Excluded System Integration

To survive judicial scrutiny under Paveit and Willowglen, Prairie's tax counsel and engineering director must first partition the project into Non-Eligible Routine Engineering (excluded from Form T661) and Eligible Experimental Development (claimed on Form T661). Mechanical mounting of COTS microwave sensors, standard PLC wiring, human-machine interface (HMI) screen programming, and baseline PID loop configuration are explicitly carved out and excluded from the SR&ED claim as routine engineering.

Next, Prairie documents the exact physical and mathematical barrier that standard signal processing and control theory cannot resolve. Inside a vibrating mobile volumetric mixer conveyor moving wet, variably compacted aggregate at 2 m/s, triboelectric static discharge, bulk-density void fluctuations, and variable clay mineral dielectric permittivity corrupt the 2.45 GHz microwave phase-shift signal, reducing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to below 6 dB. Simultaneously, pugmill auger hydraulic pressure exhibits non-linear viscoelastic hysteresis due to variable aggregate angularity, rendering standard linear PID control unstable and causing severe water-dosing oscillation and mix segregation within 10 seconds. Determining whether a real-time state-estimation algorithm can decouple bulk-density void distortion and clay dielectric polarization from true surface moisture content within a 50 ms embedded compute constraint on a vibrating mobile chassis establishes a rigorous, defensible technological uncertainty.
Step 2: Formulating Algorithmic and Mechatronic Hypotheses

Prior to writing experimental code or running test benches, Prairie's lead control systems engineer documents formal, mathematically grounded hypotheses targeting the signal corruption and viscoelastic hysteresis mechanisms. Under Hypothesis H-01, the engineering team posits that coupling dual-frequency (0.915 GHz and 2.45 GHz) microwave attenuation and phase-shift vectors with tri-axial accelerometer chassis vibration spectra inside an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) state-space model will isolate bulk-density compaction variance from free surface water permittivity, reducing moisture estimation root-mean-square error (RMSE) from ±1.5% to ±0.3% under 5 g vibration loads. Under Hypothesis H-02, the team further hypothesizes that replacing linear PID control with a non-linear Model Predictive Control (MPC) transfer function incorporating a Bingham-plastic rheological state observer driven by high-frequency (1 kHz) auger current harmonics will eliminate hydraulic lag oscillation and stabilize discharge slump and consistency variance within ±10 mm across step-changes of ±2% aggregate moisture.
Step 3: Implementing Structured Bench-Scale and Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Experimentation

Rather than jumping directly to unrepeatable field trials—the critical methodological error in Paveit Construction Inc.—Prairie structures its investigation into three controlled, repeatable experimental stages that strictly embody the scientific method. In the first stage, comprising mathematical simulation and synthetic noise injection, engineers use MATLAB and Simulink to model the dielectric state-space equations and execute Monte Carlo simulations across 500 synthetic aggregate moisture and vibration profiles, logging predicted RMSE convergence against processor execution time. In the second stage, Prairie constructs a closed-loop recirculating aggregate and pugmill test bench inside its shop facility, where engineers prepare standardized aggregate batches with precisely pre-weighed moisture contents (2% to 8%, verified via ASTM C566 oven-drying) and systematically inject controlled clay fines (0% to 5% bentonite/illite) alongside mechanical shaker vibrations ranging from 1 g to 5 g.

In the third stage, Prairie executes version-controlled iterative testing on the shop test rig. Every modification to the EKF covariance matrices and MPC cost functions is committed to a dedicated Git repository branch (sred/ekf-dielectric-decoupling), and each test run generates an automated CSV telemetry log capturing raw microwave phase and attenuation, accelerometer vectors, EKF state estimates, oven-dried ground-truth moisture, and auger torque harmonics. When Hypothesis H-01 fails at 4% clay content due to bound-water relaxation polarization at 0.915 GHz, the engineering team documents the exact physical cause of the failure in their Jira and Confluence SR&ED logs and formulates Hypothesis H-01b by introducing a Cole-Cole dielectric relaxation compensation term.
Step 4: Contemporaneous Documentation, Cost Tracking, and Contract Structuring

To ensure full compliance during a joint audit by a CRA Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and Financial Reviewer (FR), Prairie maintains a master SR&ED Evidence Matrix that cross-references every Git commit hash, Simulink model file, oscilloscope and telemetry CSV log, and ASTM C566 oven-dry validation sheet to the specific hypothesis (H-01, H-01b, H-02) tested during each two-week engineering sprint. For financial compliance, aggregate, cement, and admixtures mixed on the shop test rig and subsequently dumped to waste after rheological testing are documented with disposal weight tickets and claimed as "materials consumed" in SR&ED on Form T661 Line 320, while custom-fabricated dual-frequency waveguide prototypes destroyed during high-vibration fatigue testing are similarly documented with scrap records. Conversely, the commercial mobile mixer truck chassis itself is excluded from material claims as a capital or commercial asset, ensuring that any eligible capital property is claimed only as a capital expenditure under paragraph 37(1)(b) of the ITA, as restored by the Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1 (S.C. 2026, c. 3), and strict adherence to Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) salary-base allocation rules. Finally, when the prototype controller is eventually mounted on a mobile mixer for a 5-day field validation trial, Prairie conducts the validation strictly on internal non-commercial test pours or under a dedicated R&D Beta Validation Agreement where no commercial consideration is paid for the controller, ensuring zero contract payment reductions under subsection 127(18) of the ITA.

body.text: 5. Strategic Conclusions for Canadian SR&ED Claimants and Advisors

The Tax Court of Canada's decision in Paveit Construction Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 129, reinforces a fundamental doctrinal truth in Canadian tax law: technical complexity, operational difficulty, and novelty to the claimant's business do not equal "experimental development" under subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. When industrial, manufacturing, or construction enterprises innovate within field processes—such as mobile roller-compacted concrete placement—they face a heightened evidentiary burden to prove that their activities transcended established industry knowledge and routine trial-and-error adaptation.

For Canadian legal counsel, accountants, and technical tax advisors, three overarching compliance imperatives emerge from Paveit Construction Inc. and its 2025–2026 companion jurisprudence in Tuna Temple Inc., Willowglen Systems, and Vortex Energy Services. First, claimants must front-load objective baseline benchmarking, as a taxpayer cannot prove "technological uncertainty" or "technological advancement" without first establishing where the boundary of standard industry practice lies. Every SR&ED project file must begin with a documented technical baseline demonstrating why existing engineering standards, published literature, and equipment specifications cannot resolve the specific system-level conflict encountered. Second, claimants must replace field trial-and-error with structured experimental design. Because reactive parameter tweaking on an active field unit or production line is likely to be treated by the Tax Court as trial and error rather than the scientific method, as in Paveit, claimants must institutionalize the scientific method by formulating written causal hypotheses prior to testing, isolating independent variables via controlled experimental matrices, and systematically analyzing failed iterations. Third, claimants must anchor oral testimony in contemporaneous documentary artifacts. Retrospective narratives drafted by external consultants during Form T661 preparation cannot cure the absence of contemporaneous experimental records, and when retrospective T661 descriptions overstate the scientific rigour of field operations, they expose company witnesses to challenge under Crown cross-examination (in Paveit, the witness was found credible, but his candid concessions undercut the claim, and the agent who prepared the claim could not double as an expert). Embedding mandatory hypothesis-and-test logging directly into daily engineering workflows—while maintaining strict physical and contractual separation from commercial production—remains the most reliable mechanism (the only sure-fire one, in the words of the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie) to safeguard Canadian SR&ED claims against reassessment and litigation.

outcome: Appeal dismissed; taxpayer failed to establish objective technological uncertainty or distinguish work from routine engineering.
